dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: A mine is not designed from the grade. It is designed from the shape of the orebody and the strength of the rock around it.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: First question: open pit, or underground?

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: By the strip ratio: tonnes of waste per tonne of ore. Near surface a pit wins. Deeper, the pit must widen to reach the ore, so waste grows with the square of depth.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Flat, wide and shallow: a pit. Steep, narrow and deep: underground. Many mines are both — a pit first, then a decline beneath it.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Design the pit, and geotechnics sets every angle.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Bench height matches the equipment. Berms catch rockfall. And benches and berms together average out to the overall slope angle — which is not chosen. It is derived.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Competent granite might hold fifty-five degrees. A weathered shear zone might demand thirty.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Underground, the structure chooses the method.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: A steep, narrow vein. Too thin to drive machines into. Longhole stoping, from levels above and below, keeping the opening the width of the vein — because every centimetre of wall is waste you pay to hoist and mill.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: A thick, steep body in strong rock. Sublevel open stoping: large voids, high productivity, low cost, with pillars or backfill holding the walls.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: A flat, tabular body. Stoping needs gravity, and gravity does not help here. So room and pillar — and the gold in the pillars stays there.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Weak rock, or a wide shear that will not stand. Cut and fill: take a slice, backfill it, stand on that, take the next. Slow, expensive, and sometimes the only thing that works.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Then the structures that complicate it. A fault offsets the ore — find the continuation before you design around a hole. A fold closes two limbs together: thicker, richer, awkward to drill.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: A dyke splits one stope into two. And a weak hangingwall flattens your slopes and raises your strip ratio — enough, on its own, to send the whole mine underground.

dialogue.speaker: juma
dialogue.text: So where does the design actually start?

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: With the geology. It always did.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Every decision in this series traces back to one thing: hot fluid moved along a structure and dropped its metal. Get the geology right, and the mine designs itself.
